newsitem.title: UK: Caspian says CBA deal will make it more competitive.
newsitem.headline: Caspian says CBA deal will make it more competitive.

text.p: Caspian Securities will be able to compete better with larger investment banks with capital behind them when the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) takes a stake in the firm, its chief executive said on Wednesday.
"A special purpose vehicle will be established to enable us to be competitive with those with large balance sheets on certain transactions," Caspian's Christopher Heath told Reuters.

Heath, who founded emerging markets investments specialist Caspian in 1995, said CBA's 17 percent holding was an investment stake which would enable Caspian to "lift its game significantly" and expand in underwriting deals, derivatives and other structures.
This would mean taking on an additional 140 to 150 staff "over the next year or so", particularly in Asia where Heath said he saw good business opportunities.
Caspian employs 260 people around the world and has offices in New York, London, Latin America and Asia. It plans to open offices in Taipei and Manila this year.

Neither party detailed the cost of CBA's stake in Caspian or who it had been bought from but banking sources said the Australian bank had paid around $25 million for the holding. The deal is expected to be completed within a month.

Caspian has said in the past that it aims to increase its capital base to $250 million from around $170 million. This expansion is expected to take place in the coming months as additional shareholders take stakes in the firm.

Heath said the group did want to increase the number of shareholders and talks had been held with four other groups interested in taking stakes. He declined to identify which groups were involved or what part of the world they were based in.

Existing shareholders in Caspian include Korea's Ssangong Investment and Securities, Thailand's National Finance and Securities, Mexican brokerage Vector Casa de Bolsa and Singapore's Philip Securities.
Heath said CBA's involvement in Caspian was a strong vote of confidence in both the firm's achievements to date and its prospects for the future.
But Caspian has no plans to give up its independence or its partnership culture and will not seek a stock exchange listing in the immediate future, although it is likely to do so in the longer term.
"We only started 18 months ago and have only been trading for 15 months...it's too early (for a listing) in our view," he said.
Heath acknowledged that it had been harder to build the Caspian name in some parts of the business than he had anticipated but the brand was now beginning to build.

A lively atmosphere of mergers and takeovers in the financial services industry in general and the investment banking arena in particular had also caused some outside uncertainty about Caspian's prospects.

"Our size perhaps worked against us," he said, adding that as Caspian had built out its business some people's confidence in the firm's ability to survive had been dented by the environment of larger firms making aggressive bids for smaller ones.
CBA's head of institutional banking Michael Katz said in a joint statement that the deal emphasised his division's "focus on high value investment banking products and services".
Katz said CBA expected to work with Caspian "across a broad range of activity including debt and equity capital markets, corporate finance, research and product development".

Both firms said the deal would bring mutual benefits principally in Asia and would provide additional distribution for CBA's institutional banking products into Asia through Caspian's offices in Hong Kong and elsewhere in the region.
